text: Everything in this course up to now, exact amplitudes, exact probabilities, inspecting a state vector mid-circuit, is available because every example ran on a noiseless mathematical simulation. Real quantum hardware gives up several of those conveniences at once, and knowing exactly which ones is the difference between a circuit that works in theory and one that works on an actual device.

A simulated Hadamard gate produces exactly 1 over root 2 every single time. Real hardware has gate errors, where a physical pulse lands slightly off the ideal rotation, readout errors, where a measurement reports the wrong bit, and decoherence, where a qubit's state slowly degrades over time. Every additional sequential layer is more real time elapsed, which is more opportunity for decoherence to corrupt the result — on a simulator, by contrast, depth only affects how long the simulation takes to run, never whether the answer is correct.

A simulator can print the exact probability of every outcome directly. Real hardware can only sample: one full run of the circuit, called a shot, ending in one collapsed measurement. Simulating 1,000 shots of a Bell-state measurement, whose true probabilities are exactly 0.5 and 0.5, gave 487 and 513 in practice — not a bug, just what finite sampling looks like, and exactly what running the same circuit 1,000 times on real hardware would produce.

A simulator's CNOT function works identically no matter which two qubit indices you pass in. Real hardware has no such freedom — physical qubits sit in a fixed layout, and a two-qubit gate usually only works directly between physically adjacent qubits. If a circuit needs two non-adjacent qubits to interact, extra SWAP gates have to be inserted first, costing extra depth and extra exposure to errors — which is why the same logical circuit can run with meaningfully different real-world fidelity on two different devices.
The closing lesson of this course assembles everything built so far, state vectors, gates, CNOT, probabilities, and shot sampling, into one small, complete, runnable simulator core.
